title: Arsenal Reminded of the One Thing Even Mikel Arteta Can’t Control
subtitle: SI
paragraphs: By Grey WhitebloomNov 24, 2026Mikel Arteta was left to lament the most fickle of fates. / Ben Stansall/AFP/Getty ImagesLONDON — The famed chess grandmaster Savielly Tartakower once said: “Chess, that game of logic par excellence, consists of luck, luck and more luck.” The same could very much be said about soccer, perhaps without the logic.

Mikel Arteta is a manager who strives to diminish the role of fortune, good or bad, with every action he takes from the helm of Arsenal. This is a coach who prepared his players for real world travel delays by deliberately disrupting their preseason schedule, forcing the team bus on circuitous routes and holding back team meals so that everyone is on their toes at all times, even for dinner.

Yet, try as he might, even Arteta cannot bend the cosmic fates to his will. He cannot stop David Raya picking up an injury from an innocuous fall or guarantee that Viktor Gyökeres converts a header from point-blank range with the Borussia Dortmund goal at his mercy. All he can do is put his players in a position to have the best chance of succeeding, cross his fingers and hope.

Despite the frustrations which will come from a second successive draw in the Champions League on Tuesday night, Arteta can take pride in the way he presented his team at the altar of the gods of good luck. As the manager claimed himself, that sense of steeliness which usually accompanies anything other than a win distinctly lacking, it was “a brilliant performance.” Sometimes, the gods simply don’t smile upon you.

Viktor Gyökeres had a match-high seven shots. / Justin Setterfield/Getty ImagesThere was a snarl and snap to the way Arsenal started against Dortmund in this Champions League league phase clash, charging around with the same crispness as the air in north London. Two Dortmund players hadn’t completed a single pass by the time Gyökeres thumped the hosts into a thoroughly deserved 10th-minute lead.
That vicious dipping effort which looped over Gregor Kobel with a crackle in the night sky was comfortably Arsenal’s hardest chance of the evening. They would squander far more presentable openings.

Gyökeres himself was guilty of the most glaring miss, stooping in the 75th minute to steer a header wide of goal from five yards out. That was one of 30 efforts that Arsenal racked up against the current Bundesliga leaders, yet only four were on target.

The Gunners amassed an xG of 2.32—Dortmund couldn’t get past one—and took an outrageous 56 touches in their visitors’ penalty box. Noni Madueke and Gyökeres alone had more possession in the opposition 18-yard area (24 touches) than the entire visiting team combined (23).
"We could have won the game in many different ways,” Gyökeres fairly surmised post-match. “We played well and created a lot of chances, we deserved to win the game, but sometimes it is like that.”
As Arteta repeatedly throughout his postmatch press conference: “There is an element of luck.”

Dortmund’s rise to the summit of the Bundesliga, sitting above the imperious Bayern Munich with an unbeaten record from 10 matches, is built on their defensive solidity. Only one team in Europe’s top five leagues can match their miserly record of just seven goals conceded: Arsenal.
Yet, the parsimonious outfit was flummoxed by the dizzying rotation of personnel from their hosts. Gyökeres’s opener serves as a perfect example.

Dortmund captain Nico Schlotterbeck is left to lament the room Arsenal’s striker was afforded on the edge of the box, but he and his fellow center back, Waldemar Anton, had been forced to drop off by Ben White’s run into the box. That’s the same Ben White who started the evening as Arsenal’s right back making a typical center forward’s run.

Arsenal’s fullbacks were everywhere. / Amazon Prime VideoWhite’s opposite fullback Piero Hincapié also spent much of the contest bursting beyond Dortmund’s backline, stretching the vertical height of the visitors like a black and yellow accordion at full extension. This created ample room between the lines for Gyökeres and, in particular, Martin Ødegaard to wreak havoc; Arsenal’s captain racked up a prodigious nine chances created—yet none of them were converted.

Madueke skewed wide on multiple occasions, Declan Rice clanked the post, and a meaty wall of Dortmund shirts managed to guard the goal line on the rare occasions when Kobel was bypassed. Somehow, the ball only found the net once.

Hincapié and White were simply fulfilling the same versatile briefs that Riccardo Calafiori and Jurriën Timber carried out so well against Newcastle United on Saturday. Much like in midweek, Arsenal’s attacking dominance was only rewarded with a draw.
“It was unbelievable that sometimes the ball doesn’t end up in the back of the net,” Arteta sighed on Tuesday. “How in hell, some of the balls haven’t gone inside, I don’t know.”

Kepa Arrizabalaga had a strong game. / Nigel French/Sportsphoto/Allstar/Getty ImagesArsenal’s wastefulness in front of goal has been a feature of the season, but Arteta was presented with a new problem to solve against Dortmund: his goalkeeper. David Raya
The absence of Arsenal’s injured first-choice goalkeeper had prompted much hand-wringing about the prospect of the Gunners being forced to turn to their distinctly inferior No. 2, Kepa Arrizabalaga.
